title: Mutations, PCR and Biotechnology
seo_title: Year 12 Biology: Mutations and Biotechnology Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Biology Unit 3: DNA, genes and the continuity of life
standard_text: Point and chromosomal mutations and their effects; mutagens; restriction enzymes, ligase and recombinant DNA; PCR; gel electrophoresis and DNA profiling; gene editing with CRISPR; uses and ethics of biotechnology. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 3: Heredity and continuity of life)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Biology worksheets on mutations and biotechnology: point and frameshift mutations, restriction enzymes, plasmids, PCR, gel electrophoresis, DNA profiling, CRISPR and GMOs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: PCR doubles DNA each cycle: 2ⁿ copies after n cycles.
key_sub: In a gel, small fragments move further.
body_html:
How to think about it

Mutations change the DNA sequence. A substitution may change one amino acid (or none: silent); an insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame. Mutations are the source of new alleles.

Gene technology uses restriction enzymes to cut DNA and ligase to join it, for example into a plasmid. PCR copies DNA (2ⁿ copies after n cycles). Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size, as in DNA profiling. CRISPR-Cas9 edits a chosen sequence.

Example

1 DNA molecule, 10 PCR cycles. Copies?

2¹⁰

Answer: 1024

Example

3000 bp DNA cut at 1200. Fragments?

1200 and 3000 − 1200

Answer: 1200 bp and 1800 bp

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all mutations are harmful.
  • Saying larger DNA fragments move further in a gel.
  • Forgetting that PCR needs primers and a heat-stable polymerase.

faq.q: Why is a frameshift mutation usually worse than a substitution?
faq.a: It changes every codon after the mutation, so many amino acids change and a stop codon may appear early.
Short tandem repeats are copied by PCR and separated by size; the pattern of bands identifies people for forensics and paternity testing.

items.q:
Kai compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: GTACGAAATT
After: GTAGCGAAATT
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: An extra base was added, so the sequence is longer.

items.q: What is a tumour suppressor gene?
c: a gene that makes cells divide faster
a gene that slows cell division; if mutated, cells can divide uncontrollably
a gene that only works in plants
items.e: For example the gene for p53.

items.q: mRNA: AUUAUGAUU. Codons: AUG = Met, AUU = Ile, UAU = Tyr, GCA = Ala. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AUU AUG AUU.

items.q: What do restriction enzymes do?
c: cut DNA at specific base sequences
items.e: They often leave sticky ends.

items.q: What is the genome of an organism?
items.e: The proteome is the set of proteins it can make.

items.q:
Ruby compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: TTAGTCATTGG
After: TTAGTATTGG
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: A base was removed, so the sequence is shorter.

items.q:
Chloe compares a DNA sequence before and after a mutation.
Before: ATTCGCTTTTTC
After: ATTCGCTTTTTTC
What kind of mutation is it?
items.e: An extra base was added, so the sequence is longer.

items.q: How can a substitution mutation stop a protein working?
c: it may change an amino acid in the active site so the shape changes
it always makes the protein longer
items.e: Or it may create a stop codon.

items.q: mRNA: GAUUGGUCU. Codons: GAU = Asp, UCU = Ser, UGG = Trp, GCU = Ala, CGU = Arg. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: GAU UGG UCU.

items.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9 used for?
c: editing a specific DNA sequence by cutting it with a guide RNA
items.e: It can knock out or change genes.

items.q: mRNA: UUCCAAAUG. Codons: AUG = Met, CAA = Gln, UUC = Phe. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: UUC CAA AUG.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with embryonic stem cells?
c: embryos are destroyed to obtain them
items.e: iPS cells avoid this.

items.q: What is a recombinant plasmid?
c: a bacterial plasmid with a gene from another organism inserted into it
items.e: Used to make insulin in bacteria.

items.q: What is a silent mutation?
c: a mutation that stops all transcription
a mutation that changes many amino acids
a base change that does not change the amino acid, because the code is degenerate
items.e: The protein is unchanged.

items.q: In gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode?
c: they are attracted by the dye
DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
items.e: Smaller fragments move further.

items.q: What is a transcription factor?
c: a protein that binds to DNA and switches transcription of a gene on or off
an enzyme that joins amino acids
items.e: It binds near the gene's promoter.

items.e: An extra base was added, so the sequence is longer.

items.q: What is a genetically modified organism (GMO)?
c: an organism with a natural mutation
an organism bred by selective breeding only
an organism whose DNA has been changed using gene technology
a cloned organism with no changes
items.e: Bt cotton is widely grown in Australia.

items.q: How can genetically modified bacteria make human insulin?
c: bacteria are fused with human cells
the human insulin gene is put into a plasmid and inserted into the bacteria
items.e: The bacteria are grown in fermenters.

items.q: What does in vivo gene cloning use?
c: vectors such as plasmids to put genes into host cells
items.e: In vitro cloning uses PCR.

items.q: Why are the same restriction enzymes used to cut the gene and the plasmid?
c: so they have complementary sticky ends
so they are the same length
items.e: The ends can then base pair.

items.q: What does DNA ligase do?
c: joins DNA fragments by forming bonds between nucleotides
items.e: It seals a gene into a plasmid.

items.q: What is genetic screening used for?
c: finding people who carry particular alleles
items.e: Genetic counselling then explains the risks.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1450. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2400): 1450, 950. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What does reverse transcriptase do?
c: makes cDNA from a mRNA template
items.e: Used to make genes without introns.

items.q: What do restriction endonucleases do?
c: cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
items.e: Many leave sticky ends.

items.q: Why does an insertion or deletion of one base usually have a big effect?
c: it changes only one amino acid
it shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
items.e: This is a frameshift mutation.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 950, 1000, 1600. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2000): 950, 600, 400, 50. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1500 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 550. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1500): 950, 550. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Why is PCR heated to about 95 °C?
c: to separate the DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
items.e: Primers anneal at about 55 °C; extension at 72 °C.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 200. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2400): 2200, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What are primers in PCR?
c: short single strands of DNA that bind to the start of the target sequence
RNA molecules that carry amino acids
items.e: DNA polymerase starts from them.

items.q: What is a mutagen?
c: a factor that increases the rate of mutation, such as UV radiation or some chemicals
items.e: Australia has high UV levels and high skin cancer rates.

items.q: Why are mutations important for evolution?
c: they are the original source of new alleles and genetic variation
items.e: Most are neutral; some are harmful, a few helpful.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with genetic testing?
c: privacy: insurers or employers might use the results
items.e: Genetic counselling helps people decide.

items.q: Why is Bt cotton grown in Australia?
c: it contains a bacterial gene that makes a protein toxic to caterpillar pests, reducing insecticide use
items.e: Insecticide sprays fell by up to 85%.

items.q: Why is a promoter added with a gene in genetic engineering?
c: so RNA polymerase can bind and the gene is transcribed
items.e: A terminator is added to stop it.

items.q: What are the three temperature steps in each PCR cycle?
items.e: A heat-stable polymerase (Taq) is used.

items.q: What is genetic fingerprinting based on?
c: variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), which differ between people
genes that are the same in everyone
items.e: The pattern of bands is compared.

items.q: PCR starts with 3 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 20 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 3 × 220 = 3145728.

items.q: PCR starts with 3 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 10 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 3 × 210 = 3072.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 2 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 50 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 25 cycles; amount × 225 = 33554432.

items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 5 × 26 = 320.

items.e: 20 cycles; amount × 220 = 1048576.

items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 50 × 212 = 204800.

items.q: PCR starts with 3 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 12 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 3 × 212 = 12288.

items.q: What is a point mutation?
c: the loss of a whole chromosome
a change in a protein only
a change in a single base, by substitution, insertion or deletion
a change in the number of chromosome sets
items.e: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by one base substitution.

items.q: PCR starts with 5 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 3 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 5 × 23 = 40.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 5 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 50 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 10 cycles; amount × 210 = 1024.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 2 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 60 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 30 cycles; amount × 230 = 1073741824.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 5 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 75 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 15 cycles; amount × 215 = 32768.

items.q: What is a sticky end?
c: a short single-stranded overhang left by some restriction enzymes
items.e: Complementary sticky ends can join.

items.q: What is the role of PCR?
c: to make millions of copies of a DNA sequence
items.e: Each cycle doubles the DNA.

items.q: PCR starts with 3 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 25 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 3 × 225 = 1.01 × 108.

items.q: What is a DNA probe used for?
c: finding a specific allele by binding to a complementary sequence
items.e: Probes are labelled with fluorescent or radioactive markers.

items.q: Which is a use of genetic fingerprinting?
items.e: Also forensics and checking breeding plans.

items.q: How is DNA profiling used in forensic science?
c: reading a person's whole genome every time
comparing the lengths of short tandem repeats from crime-scene DNA and suspects
items.e: STR patterns are almost unique to each person.

items.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?

items.e: It comes from a bacterium in hot springs.

items.q: What is epigenetics?

items.e: For example DNA methylation.

items.q: Why can different cells in one body make different proteins?

items.e: All body cells have the same genome.
